results.title: Forecasting war is different to forecasting a coin flip
results.content: Forecasts are subjective probabilities. As of today (May 28, 2022), Metaculus says there’s a 35% probability for a nuclear weapon to be detonated in war in the next 28 years. Imagine it’s 2072 and no such detonation has happened. It is very likely, I think, that the community will consider such an event to be less than 35% likely in the next 28 year period (that is, by 2100). Perhaps, having seen the continuing absence of nuclear weapons used in war, they might now say there’s just a 15% of [...] weapon will be detonated in an act of war by 2050. rationale: Starting from historical base rates, there have been no clearly confirmed AI-enabled mass-casualty catastrophes yet, but wars, pandemics and infrastructure failures provide substantial background opportunities for AI to become a material enabler as it diffuses. I assign most near-term risk at the lower rungs to military/cyber/infrastructure misuse and most high-rung risk to AI-enabled bio, nuclear-escalation pathways, and loss of control; current evidence suggests real capability growth but still major practical barriers and some improving governance. By 2050 and especially 2100, pervasive AI deployment and a meaningful chance of transformative systems make the cumulative tail much larger, while the extinction rung remains below broader “AI catastrophe” estimates because it requires literal extinction or near-extinction rather than severe collapse.

results.title: Why do Experts Disagree on Existential Risk and P(doom)? A Survey of AI Experts
results.content: Prominent AI researchers hold dramatically different views on the degree of risk from building AGI. For example, Dr. Roman Yampolskiy estimates a 99% chance of an AI-caused existential catastrophe[Dr. Roman Yampolskiy [@romanyam] 2024](#bib.bib4) (often called “P(doom)”) whereas others such as Yann Lecun believe that this probability is effectively zero[Yann LeCun [@ylecun] 2023](#bib.bib5). The goal of the survey is to understand what drives this massive divergence in views on AI risk among [...] Several existing surveys have examined AI expert beliefs. The largest is the AI Impacts Survey(Grace et al. 2024), which surveys thousands of authors at the NeurIPS conference. AI Impacts asked experts questions such as “when will AI exceed human performance,” in response, the median expert answered 2061, and 10% answered 2026. According to AI Impacts, roughly 40% of respondents indicated a >10% chance of catastrophic outcomes from AI progress. Other surveys also seek to answer when experts [...] Today, many prominent AI researchers including Nobel Laureate Geoffrey Hinton and Turing Laureate Yoshua Bengio argue that intelligent machines could endanger human civilizationBengio et al. 2024. In May of 2023, many of the most notable scientists and figures in AI signed a statement stating, “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war”(noauthor\_center\_2023 2023).

rationale: I start from the modern base rate: confirmed deliberate biological attacks and lab accidents have caused deaths far below 1,000 since WWII, so near-term probabilities are low; however, state programs, historical wartime use, and rapidly improving synthetic biology/AI capabilities make the future hazard appreciably above the historical rate. I model the hazard as rising through mid-century as biological design and access diffuse, partly offset by surveillance, vaccines, and synthesis-screening improvements, with attribution requirements reducing effective resolution probabilities. The tail falls steeply because killing hundreds of millions to billions requires a rare combination of high transmissibility, high lethality, immune/vaccine escape, delayed response, and/or multiple releases; extinction is much lower still because biological agents are unlikely to reach every isolated population and survivors would adapt and countermeasure over time.

I anchor on expert distributions (≈0.3% baseline annual risk of a 100k-death human-caused epidemic, rising with capabilities), discounting the most inflated survey figures (which imply implausibly high 30%/10% chances). Probabilities fall steeply with each death threshold since global-scale spread requires both high transmissibility and lethality that current/near-term actors struggle to engineer, and rise over time as capabilities diffuse. Extinction remains extremely unlikely because a pathogen killing essentially everyone faces strong selection and countermeasure pressures, but I keep a nonzero tail (~0.4% by 2100) reflecting genuine deep uncertainty about advanced synthetic biology.

rationale: I start from base rates: events killing ≥1,000 happen almost every year; ≥100,000 events have occurred multiple times in recent decades from earthquakes/tsunamis/cyclones, wars and epidemics; and COVID-19 demonstrates that ≥10M deaths in a 5-year window is not merely historical. I then add low but material tail risk from nuclear war/nuclear winter, engineered or natural pandemics, severe conflict, AI-related catastrophe, and smaller contributions from natural hazards; this makes the century-scale upper rungs substantial but still well below the lower-rung disaster rates. Extinction is set below ≥1B deaths because many billion-death scenarios are survivable, and below broad “existential catastrophe” estimates because this question requires extinction or population under 5,000 rather than permanent loss of potential.

rationale: Lower rungs are near-certain over any multi-year window: events killing ≥1k (earthquakes, cyclones, epidemics) occur multiple times yearly, and a ≥100k event within a rolling 5-year window is nearly guaranteed (2004 tsunami, 2010 Haiti, COVID). ≥1M is crossed by severe pandemics/wars roughly once per generation (COVID excess deaths ~15M already qualifies for ≥10M), so it rises from moderate by 2030 to near-certain by 2100. The ≥100M, ≥1B, and extinction rungs require civilization-scale nuclear war, engineered pandemics, or AI-driven catastrophe; I anchor these to expert-survey and Ord estimates (single-digit % for ≥1B and low-single-digit % for extinction by 2100), keeping tail probabilities nonzero but small and growing with horizon as advanced-technology risks accumulate. Probabilities are non-decreasing across 2030→2050→2100 for every threshold.

## Conclusions

In The Precipice, I gave my best guess probabilities for the existential risk over the next 100 years in each of these areas. label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: Base rates for nuclear weapon use are derived from historical close calls and expert surveys, with superforecasters in the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) estimating an annualized risk of ~0.5% for a nuclear weapon killing >1,000 people. I adjust this slightly upward for the 2030 horizon (~0.8% annualized) to account for acute geopolitical tensions (e.g., Ukraine, Taiwan), yielding cumulative probabilities of 3.5% by 2030, 14% by 2050, and 31% by 2100 for the ≥1k threshold. Escalation dynamics suggest a high conditional probability that any use escalates to larger thresholds; I estimate a ~65-75% chance that a >1k event escalates to >100k (e.g., city targeting), with steady drop-offs for higher thresholds. For the ≥1B threshold, I align closely with XPT superforecaster estimates for a >10% population reduction (~800M people), adjusting slightly downward due to the strict "direct deaths and immediate consequences" criteria, yielding 0.2% by 2030, 1.2% by 2050, and 3.2% by 2100. Extinction remains extremely unlikely even in a full-scale exchange due to the likelihood of survivors in refuges (e.g., New Zealand) or deep bunkers, aligning with XPT superforecaster estimates of 0.001% by 2030, 0.01% by 2050, and 0.1% by 2100.

results.title: Preventing catastrophic pandemics
results.content:
### Mirror bacteria illustrate the possibility of engineered catastrophic biorisks

In December 2024, a working group of 38 scientists, including Nobel laureates, warned in a new report of a potentially catastrophic biorisk – “mirror life.”16 [...] ### Scale

Pandemics — especially engineered pandemics — pose a significant risk to humanity. Though the risk is difficult to assess, some researchers estimate that there is a greater than 1 in 10,000 chance of a biological catastrophe leading to human extinction within the next 100 years, and potentially as high as 1 in 100. (See below.) A biological catastrophe that doesn’t lead to extinction could still kill billions of people.

### Neglectedness [...] ### Neglectedness

Even in the aftermath of the COVID-19 outbreak, only modest resources are dedicated to pandemic prevention. In the US, for instance, spending on biodefence has only grown from an estimated $17 billion in 2019 to $27 billion in 2026.

One estimate in April 2024 found that global spending on mitigating and preventing disease outbreaks was around $130 billion, and that work specifically targeting the most catastrophic pandemics remained especially neglected.

results.title: Global catastrophic biological risk - EA Forum
results.content:
A global catastrophic biological risk (GCBR) is a global catastrophic risk that is biological in nature.

## Existential risks from biotechnology

Biotechnology offers potentially exciting ways to make people much better off, to find new ways to tackle disease, and to address climate change. However, because many biological systems are at least in principle self-replicating, significant modifications of some kinds could also pose serious risks. [...] ## Evaluation

80,000 Hours rates reducing global catastrophic biological risks a "highest priority area": a problem at the top of their ranking of global issues assessed by importance, tractability and neglectedness.

## Recommendations

In The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity, Toby Ord offers several policy and research recommendations for handling risks from engineered pandemics: [...] Ensure that all DNA synthesis is screened for dangerous pathogens. If full coverage can’t be achieved through self-regulation by synthesis companies, then some form of international regulation will be needed.
 Increase transparency around accidents in BSL-3 and BSL-4 laboratories.
 Develop standards for dealing with information hazards, and incorporate these into existing review processes.
 Run scenario-planning exercises for severe engineered pandemics.

Israeli commanders operating the system assumed the objectivity and accuracy of Lavender’s outputs, such that critical engagement with the machines was practically absent.
